To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the original, very dense neuronal population of neocortical grafts, derived from fetal rat brain, declines steadily after transplantation to somatosensory adult host cortex; (2) the numerical density of Gaba-positive neurons declines disproportionately larger than that Of GABA-negative nerve cell population; (3) at 90 days post-transplantation only 2.3 % of neurons are GABA-positive; (4) the numerical density Of GABA-negative neurons remains slightly above
GABAergic neurons are lost at a higher rate than non-GABAergic neurons in neocortical grafts.

The numerical density of neurons in neocortical grafts, derived from E16 rat embryos, declines continuously after transplantation, and that this decline is disproportionally larger for GABA-positive neurons than for GABA-negative nerve-cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of GABAergic neurons in neocortical tissue grafts.
the fate of transplanted fetal neocortical cells in adult hosts, with special emphasis on the fate of GABAergic neurons.
age-related changes in neocortical grafts, with a focus on GABAergic neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GABAergic system is more vulnerable than the non-GABAergic one, and that the GABA-negative system is more vulnerable to the aging process than the GABA-positive system.
GABAergic cells are more vulnerable to transplantation and to the post-transplantation period than non-GABAergic neurons.
the loss of GABA-positive nerve cells in neocortical grafts is a continuous process, whereas the decline of GABA-negative cells is completed in the first 30 post-transplantation days.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the age-dependent loss of GABA-positive nerve cells in the transplants is not only larger than that of the GABA-negative neurons but also more continuous and long lasting, while the loss of the latter is more rapid and transient.
the GABAergic system is more sensitive than the non-GABAergic one, in that the former is more severely affected in the course of transplantation.

the GABAergic system of neocortical neurons is particularly vulnerable to the transplantation procedure and that the loss of GABAergic neurons may be the major cause for the functional impairment of the transplants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the loss of neurons in the transplants is more severe in GABA-positive neurons than in the GABA-negative neurons.
the age-related loss of neurons in the grafts is not uniform.
GABA-negative neurons in the transplants survive transplantation much better than GABA-positive cells.
